subject: Chemistry
title: Nuclear Fusion: Powering the Stars
description: Learn Nuclear Fusion: Powering the Stars in one minute.

hook.text: The Sun fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second. Fusion is the energy source of every star.

buildup.text: At 15 million degrees, hydrogen nuclei move fast enough to overcome electromagnetic repulsion and fuse together.

discovery.text: Four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus. The helium weighs less—the missing mass becomes pure energy via E = mc².

twist.text: Fusion releases 4 times more energy per gram than fission. But we still can't sustain it on Earth—containment is the problem.

climax.text: ITER in France is building a reactor that uses magnetic fields to contain 150-million-degree plasma. First tests aim for 2035.

punchline.text: Smash light atoms together, lose mass, gain energy. The Sun's recipe for power.

quiz.question: Why is nuclear fusion so difficult to achieve on Earth?
options: It requires extreme temperatures and we can't contain the plasma effectively
The fuel (hydrogen) is too rare on Earth
Fusion reactions produce too much radiation to be safe

details.summary: Nuclear fusion combines light atomic nuclei such as hydrogen into heavier ones like helium, releasing energy from the mass difference as described by Einstein's E equals mc squared. Fusion powers every star in the universe and promises virtually limitless clean energy if harnessed on Earth.
details.whyItMatters: Fusion could provide nearly unlimited energy with minimal radioactive waste and no carbon emissions. Achieving controlled fusion on Earth remains one of humanity's greatest scientific challenges.
takeaways: Fusion combines light nuclei and converts mass into energy
It powers the sun by fusing hydrogen into helium continuously
Controlled fusion on Earth requires extreme temperatures and pressure

faq.question: Why is it so difficult to achieve nuclear fusion on Earth?
faq.answer: Fusion requires temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei..

faq.question: When will fusion power plants become commercially available?
faq.answer: As of 2026, experimental reactors like ITER and several private ventures are making progress, but commercial fusion remains at least a decade away. The running joke is that fusion is always thirty years in the future, though recent breakthroughs have accelerated optimism.
